notes.title: Tidekeeper Weather and Worldbuilding Early Access Update
notes.notes:
Folks, welcome back! The Tidekeeper team is honored to announce that after a little over two months of development, we bring you the [b]Weather and Worldbuilding update[/b]!

So, what can you expect?
[list]
[*]Updated weather! From sunny mornings to stormy evenings, our new weather will change the way you approach navigating the Hourglass Isles. Tread carefully across the waves so that you can still make it to your tasks on time!
[*]Scrap! Behold, a brand new economy in the Hourglass Isles! Around the world, you may find little parts of scrap floating in the water. Collect scrap to build wave disruptors and spotlights to assist in your navigation.
[*]Worldbuilding bits! The environment has gotten a bit of a makeover. We hope you'll be able to find and admire the little runes, crystals, monoliths, and other decorations that give the Hourglass Isles just that little bit of extra flair!
[*]Updated camera movement! We saw your bugs in earlier builds and have updated the camera so that it's much smoother in dialogue.
[*]And finally, tons of bug fixes, polish, and tweaks.
[/list]
We hope that you'll enjoy this new update!

If you find that anything goes wrong or unexpectedly while you explore the Hourglass Isles, please use [url=https://forms.gle/ibMt8eS4AXH9sqDV7]this Google Form[/url] to report any bugs that you find.

Thank you very much for playing Tidekeeper with us. Let's get scheduling!

notes.title: Tidekeeper Art Devlog: Meet Ross and Adam!
notes.notes:
Hello hello, Tidekeeper Steam devlog! Apologies for the late posting. It's been busy at the office keeping everything moving!

Today, we are happy to introduce our two Tidekeeper artists to you: Ross and Adam! Let's get movin' right along.

----------------------
[b]Kylie[/b]: What's goin' on folks? Would you please do us the honor of introducing yourself and what you do in the Tidekeeper team?

[b]Adam[/b]: My name is Adam Chizmar and I am the art director for Tidekeeper.

[b]Ross[/b]: Hey everyone. My name is Ross Omland and I am the technical artist involved with the world building and decoration of Tidekeeper.  This involves working with the environmental props, weather, or to help create those special materials, shaders or particle systems that help make the world feel a little more alive.  For this particular game, this has been a unique challenge because it's the first time the team has decided to create a larger world that the player can navigate around in.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/60b0427e74b14aa0a4cf87482c79ea52422cbddd.png[/img]
--
[b]Kylie[/b]: That is sweet, it's great to have you both here! Let's get into some art specifics. Do you have a pipeline? As in, when you have a new task or feature, do you have a plan of how it generally goes from start to finish?

[b]Ross[/b]: Yes definitely! I usually have to work through the entire process of creating the asset before I start. Once the team has discussed what we want to create, reference material is gathered and we've come up with a basic design, I can start looking into the finer details. If a building or structure has special requirements such as moving parts, things that glow, lights that may turn on and off or even have various states to it such as being damaged or not, it can drastically alter how the item gets created so I have to plan accordingly. Once I have the overall idea, I write out a rough step-by-step plan for myself along with a list of any any optimizations that I could include which helps identify any future problems with the creation process, as well as reduces the probability of having to redo something later on down the road, because it's more difficult to make changes once the asset has been modelled and textured.

[b]Adam[/b]: For 3d assets in this project, we begin with a general discussion of what art assets might be needed and how it would fit into the story and the world we are building. After that, we find some reference materials and do some conceptual sketches. Once we get a good handle on that, it gets modeled, textured, and put into the Unity engine. From there, we tweak the materials, lighting, and any additional post effects or particles that might be needed.
With UI, it's often much more of an iterative process. That involves lots of reference, sketching layouts and styles, and testing. [i]A lot of testing[/i]. UI can be constantly evolving as the game progresses to adjust to player feedback and other necessities from in-game mechanics that might arise.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/2675e51b6064d76dd4165621d810528d17b76c8a.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/dd962b9526c8f83d756cd340b13161542e49d46a.png[/img]
--
[b]Kylie[/b]: Oh wow! It's fascinating to hear how you approach all of this. Thank you both for the time and energy you put into all your beautiful assets. :) With a more fun spin in mind, how do you find inspiration for your work as you're moving along?

[b]Adam[/b]: I found a lot of inspiration from children's adventure books I grew up with and the art styles they used, like "Davey's First Boat", "Scuffy the Tugboat", and "The Mysterious Tadpole". I also found a lot of inspiration in some artists from the past, like Tibor Gergely and Eyvind Earle, along with some more recent illustrators, like Ben Mantle. These artists and books bring a warmth, style, and life that feels like being a kid to me, and I want to infuse that feeling as much as possible into the art and story of Tidekeeper.

[b]Ross[/b]: Definitely in the details.  If there's a way to make something seem a little more alive, that catches your eye and makes you look at it for a moment longer, then I feel like I did my job.  Those details can be items that rotate such as moving fan blades, blinking lights, a banner blowing in the wind or with the use of particles for smoke or water effects.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/63187e75b479214122b22d0cb25a3ed63ea06597.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/d74fdab562af08ec99c446339becb58f00166465.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/8ce906c7e546e72979d8668af6f59d468cef5a2e.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/051a22bf83225f515334126f107df1e42a13d9e6.png[/img]
--
[b]Kylie[/b]: This is really great! These answers bring such a cozy perspective to Tidekeeper development. With inspiration found and pipelines down, what would you say is the toughest thing you've had to tackle so far in the project?

[b]Ross[/b]: There's a little town made of storage containers and scrap in the game which has been to date the most complex model I've ever worked on. The idea was to create a series of buildings, docks and props in a modular fashion so that various layouts could be created in order to fill out the shop area and to give the impression that the buildings all look a little different.  These models would share the same texture and unwrap coordinates, but use a different set of unwrap coordinates for emission textures that could be activated to light-up the town at night. Special shaders had to be created to utilize multiple UV coordinates on the same mesh which was a unique process that I hadn't done before. While this was particularly challenging for me, I'm very happy with the final results.

[b]Adam[/b]: Probably the UI. Again, it's a constantly evolving thing in this game as it expands and is tested. I think we are heading in the right direction, and I'm very proud of some of the interesting ways we tackled the unique needs and learning objectives of this game. But it still needs some more love to get it where it needs to be.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/3e3fabedeb24222a1031ed0ae0eb451e21bbb380.png[/img]
--
[b]Kylie[/b]: Holy crap! Yeah, this all sounds tough. It's incredible to hear about all the learning and experimenting and iterating happening; I hope you're both immensely proud of what you've got so far, too! Speaking of, do you have a favorite asset or feature that you've worked on so far?

[b]Adam[/b]: I love all the character artwork a lot, especially Chumby. Chumby was mishmash of sea creatures I've loved since childhood, specifically the whale shark. As a kid, I had my "shark book" that showed someone holding on to a whale shark as they swam with it and I always dreamed of doing that one day. I can't now because I think it's illegal, but I can still dream about it and live it out vicariously through this game.

[b]Ross[/b]: While it's something we're currently working to get into the game, I think having everything have a day vs night-time texture set on the various structures has been the most rewarding. When buildings light-up at sunset, plants begin to glow, and trees begin to give off an eerie light, I think it really pulls you into the world and makes it more exciting to explore.

--
[b]Kylie[/b]: Absolutely beautiful! I hope everyone will give these things some extra love and attention while they play. :D As we start to wrap up, are there any features or experiments you're excited to try out as we continue work on Tidekeeper?

[b]Ross[/b]: I know improving the movement and interactions between Chumby and Fin will become a priority for me in the near future and I'm excited to have a more dynamic partnership between the two characters as they navigate the world together. I'd very much like to add character animations and dynamic movement to Fin as you move through the water which I'm hoping will make the overall play experience much more enjoyable when exploring.

[b]Adam[/b]: I'm excited to see the world fill out more with unique locations and characters. I'm also looking forward to building out the events of the on-coming storm and what that means to the player, the story, and to the Hourglass Isles.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/6462c8f79780fe7f269a33131626c405e49f0890.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/2940658d8ec5228ee9ea9bf9826a6e84fe466c69.png[/img]
--
[b]Kylie[/b]: Thank you, thank you both so very much! Any remaining comments for the good of the cause as we sign off?

[b]Adam[/b]: I love Chumby. Chumby is my favorite.

[b]Ross[/b]: I'm definitely looking forward to working on some of the content that's coming down the pipeline for the future that I'm sure people will enjoy. More content, creatures and things for players to do!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45220111/030ef61580acd2f19e0d9da165029c10ad074331.png[/img]

notes.title: Tidekeeper Design Devlog: Meet Lawrence and our Learning Objective
notes.notes:
Folks, welcome back! The Tidekeeper team is pleased to announce that we had a lot of fun brainstorming over the last two weeks, and we are excitedly continuing development.

While we're working on our next update we want to release to you all, we thought it'd be fun to do some interviews with our developers to get a little insight into making a game!

Today, we are meeting Lawrence, the designer behind Tidekeeper. But, we'll let him talk about all that. Take it away!

----------------------

[b]Kylie[/b]: Hey there! My name is Kylie, and I'm the producer for Tidekeeper. Today, I'm talking with Lawrence. Could you please give us an intro into who you are and what you do for the Tidekeeper team?

[b]Lawrence[/b]: Sure! I'm Lawrence, one of the Game Designers at Simcoach Games. I'm the primary designer on Tidekeeper, and also contribute to narrative, writing, and audio aspects.

[b]Kylie[/b]: Thank you, thank you! And let's talk Tidekeeper. What is your elevator pitch? How would you describe the game in a sentence or two for anyone unfamiliar with the concept?

[b]Lawrence[/b]: I would say Tidekeeper is a strategic adventure game with an emphasis on scheduling and time management skills in a nautical atmospheric world (lots of buzzwords there, haha). Tidekeeper aims to teach these important life skills implicitly through core mechanics and experimentation.

[b]Kylie[/b]: That is a fascinating concept! I want to dissect the scheduling component a little bit. You mentioned Tidekeeper as [i]teaching[/i] these skills, which means that at its heart, Tidekeeper has a learning objective. How does designing a game with a learning objective compare to making one purely for entertainment purposes?

[b]Lawrence[/b]: Good question. I tend to view the learning objective as another constraint to work in and a main star much of the design can revolve around. By "constraint", I don't want to come across as if I'm shackled by the learning objective. I see constraints and pillars as beautiful fence posts which mark out the area I get to play in. It's an exciting variable that can be woven into the game's mechanics and influence the theme and/or story. While I still aim to focus on fun, challenge, and all those elements that make games enjoyable, designing a game with a learning objective provides a unique challenge in also getting the learning objective to be taught in an engaging way. It's also a little heartwarming to know that the projects I'm working on can help some players with life skills.

[b]Kylie[/b]: This sounds like a great perspective to have while designing such games! I'm sure your players appreciate the time you spend considering and testing things for their benefit. Speaking of, what would you consider to be some of the biggest challenges you've faced so far in designing Tidekeeper?

[b]Lawrence[/b]: We were fortunate to come into Tidekeeper with a defined learning objective and grounded approach of how we wanted to showcase scheduling and time management skills. I would say that some of the bigger challenges have more revolved around everything surrounding it that the player is engaging with: world, story, minigames, and all the tech that goes into these aspects. Tidekeeper is a relatively large game for us historically. While we're all excited to grow the Hourglass Isles and deliver our full vision, a challenge for me has been to gauge how much to grow, what to grow, and how much we want to tackle as a team. I am by no means the final say; we are a pretty democratic team, but striving for balance and for aspects to not get lost or watered down in additional mechanics and features has been my latest hurdle.

[b]Kylie[/b]: I can definitely understand that. At some point you'll have to reach a limit, but finding it seems really tough! You got this, though. As we're starting to wrap up, what would you say you're looking forward to the most as we continue development?

[b]Lawrence[/b]: Our big push with these new additions to Tidekeeper has been to serve the environment and world of the game. We're all very excited to amplify the world and really make it feel like a living place. Filling in the gaps from our first deployment and exemplifying our vision of what the Hourglass Isles are and can be is a very exciting prospect and one the entire team is amped to deliver!

[b]Kylie[/b]: This sounds exciting!! Thank you! Is there anything else you want to mention for the good of the cause before we sign off?

[b]Lawrence[/b]: Everyone here is looking forward to making wonderful experiences for you! We want you to learn and have fun!

notes.title: Tidekeeper Development Revival!
notes.notes:
Welcome back to the Hourglass Isles! The Tidekeeper team is resuming development on the game beginning today, February 20, 2025.

We are bringing to the table a backlog influenced by early feedback and playtester wishes. From a new weather system to more incentives to explore the Hourglass Isles, we're aiming to flesh Tidekeeper out and make it an even better experience over the next few months. While the game's main purpose is still to support education and skill-building, we think it has a lot of potential to be something general audiences can enjoy, as well.

Some of our team's current goals include:
[list]
[*]Post our first devlog (check!)
[*]Begin work on the weather system (watch out for those storms!)
[*]Clean up our current code and systems in order to make all the cool, new stuff easier to implement (someone find my rubber ducky!)
[*]Brainstorm new ideas for more minigames that players can encounter in tasks around the world (my mind is just [i]racing[/i] with all the possibilities!)
[/list]

We will release new content when it feels most appropriate; what we mean by this is that the game will have changed in such a significant way, and has been properly tested, that we feel comfortable sharing it with a wider audience for more feedback. This should generally be when we hit major milestones (ex. the weather system is complete and changes how players would interact with the game compared to the current version).

We will be posting these devlogs as we move along to keep everyone up to date with the game's progress. We thank you for your patience at the first early access release of Tidekeeper, and look forward to seeing it take shape based on everyone's feedback!

Signing off for now,
Kylie (Tidekeeper producer)
